newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Sea reactors run normally despite oil spill.
newsitem.headline: Japan Sea reactors run normally despite oil spill.

text.p: Nuclear reactors along the Sea of Japan coast are operating normally despite having to put up special fences to stop slicks from an oil spill from reaching their intake pipes, power company officials said on Monday.
"The reactors are running at full capacity," said a spokesman for Kansai Electric Power Co Inc.
Kansai Electric operates 11 pressurised water reactors, with a total capacity of 9.8 million kilowatts (kw), on Wakasa Bay on the Sea of Japan coast.
It is the world's largest concentration of nuclear reactors.
Oil fences that the firm put up last week have successfully kept the oil slicks from the intake pipes, the spokesman said.
The seawater is used as a coolant in the plants.
Concern about the nuclear plants began several days after the 13,157-tonne tanker Nakhodka broke up in rough seas on January 2, spreading tonnes of oil across a 450-km (285-mile) stretch of coast.

Maritime officials have no firm figure on how much oil has escaped, but said an earlier estimate of 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) was too low. The 26-year-old tanker was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil.
Another nuclear plant operator, the Japan Atomic Power Co, has two reactors on the bay but one is undergoing maintenance checks and the other has been closed since late last month for repairs.
The Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp also has two reactors on the bay.
One, a prototype fast-breeder reactor, has been shut since a sodium coolant leakage accident in December 1995, and the other was closed on Monday evening for routine maintenance.
